learningObjective: Use natural-frequency branches to see why a rare prior can make false positives outnumber true positives even when sensitivity and specificity are both 99 percent.
mediumRationale: A deterministic SVG is the smallest medium that can preserve the two population branches, their different base sizes, and their reunion in the positive-test denominator. Fixed integer counts make every quantity checkable without scripting.

mediumComparison.mermaid: Rejected: a flowchart can show branches but does not provide the precise, compact quantitative hierarchy needed to compare 99 true positives with 999 false positives.
mediumComparison.svg: Selected: deterministic positions, direct count labels, distinct branch outlines, and an explicit fraction make the denominator visible and remain legible in one narrow-column panel.
mediumComparison.semanticHtml: Rejected: a table would expose the counts but not emphasize that two very unequal prior populations feed the same positive-result pool.
mediumComparison.interaction: Rejected: changing prevalence could be useful in a calculator, but controls and state are unnecessary for the single base-rate lesson in this article.
mediumComparison.paperReuse: Rejected: no reuse permission was established for the primary paper, textbook figures, clinical-review tables, or local deck artwork. The implementation uses original geometry and the article's independently calculated example.
mediumComparison.noVisual: Rejected: the prose gives the correct equation and result, but readers must mentally construct why the false-positive term dominates the denominator.

pages.insight: The preceding parametric-models slide distinguishes observed, transformed, and latent-variable models but contains no Bayes update or base-rate example.
The directly relevant slide labels prior, likelihood, posterior, and evidence around Bayes' rule; its general inference overview does not show how unequal prior populations contribute to a posterior.
The neighboring learning slide contrasts MLE, Bayesian estimation, and MAP and reinforces that Bayesian parameters retain distributions rather than only point estimates.
The following VAE slide applies Bayes' rule to an intractable latent posterior but adds no diagnostic-testing or natural-frequency treatment.

deckReview.notes: The complete 214-page local deck was text-indexed for Bayes, posterior, likelihood, prior, medical, diagnosis, disease, and prevalence. Pages 79-82 were then rendered and visually inspected as the full relevant neighborhood. Page 80 is the only general Bayes-rule overview; none of these slides teaches the article's rare-disease denominator. No deck image, icon, wording, or layout is reused.

sourceReview.notes: The hardest mental model is the positive-result denominator under a rare prior. The visual converts the article's own probabilities into an original cohort of 100,000 expected cases: 100 have disease and yield 99 true positives; 99,900 are healthy and yield 999 false positives; therefore 99 of 1,098 positive results, about 9 percent, are true positives. These are exact arithmetic consequences of the article's synthetic assumptions, not empirical clinical claims.

agentReview.summary: Independently reviewed the complete article, text-indexed all 214 deck pages, visually inspected pages 79-82, and checked an authoritative textbook, a primary frequency-format paper, and an authoritative clinical review before selecting an original natural-frequency funnel.

implementation.accessibility: The SVG has a linked title and detailed description containing every branch count and the final fraction. Direct labels identify diseased, healthy, true-positive, and false-positive groups; different box outlines, positions, arrows, and written arithmetic preserve the lesson without color. A 360-unit viewBox scales to the article column without a minimum width, established theme tokens preserve dark-mode contrast, and shared print rules enforce a light high-contrast palette.
